title: Authentication and Authorization for Frontend Developers
description: Understand sessions, browser credential risks, OAuth/OIDC roles, and why API authorization cannot live only in the UI.
learningOutcomes: Explain session, cookie and token risks relevant to browser applications.
Describe OAuth authorization-code + PKCE and the role of OpenID Connect.
Compare SPA token handling with a BFF architecture.
Build a test matrix that exercises server-side authorization rather than only route guards.

blocks.text: Authentication, authorization, and the frontend trust boundary

Authentication answers 'who are you?'; authorization answers 'may this identity perform this action on this resource?'. A frontend can guide navigation and hide unavailable actions, but client code is controlled by the user. The API/data layer must enforce access on every protected operation. A route guard improves user experience; it is not a security boundary.

blocks.title: Never trust a client-only permission check
blocks.text: A user can alter JavaScript, replay a request or call an endpoint outside the UI. Do not ship privileged API keys in a browser bundle. Enforce authorization at the trusted server/data layer and test direct requests as well as the normal screen flow.

items: A server-backed session typically keeps session state on the server and gives the browser an opaque session identifier; the identifier is a credential and must be protected.

Cookie attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite reduce specific risks, but they are not a complete security design. Cookie-authenticated state-changing requests need an explicit CSRF strategy appropriate to the application.
Tokens are credentials, not just strings to decode. A JWT payload is commonly readable by its holder; decoding the payload does not verify the signature or decide whether the token should be trusted.

Any credential readable by frontend JavaScript can be exposed by an XSS compromise. Avoid universal 'always use localStorage' or 'cookies solve everything' rules; make the storage choice against the threat model, framework and server architecture.
Logout, expiration, rotation/revocation, session fixation, XSS and CSRF belong in the threat model—not only login-form validation.

blocks.code:
Browser / SPA -> Authorization Server
  1. Start authorization-code flow with PKCE
  2. User authenticates and grants access
  3. Client exchanges code + PKCE verifier
  4. Client uses access token for API requests
API -> validates credential + permissions -> returns data

OIDC adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0.
An ID token and an access token serve different purposes.

steps.title: Separate the roles in the flow
steps.explanation: The authorization server authenticates the user and issues protocol responses; the API/resource server still validates the credential and enforces authorization. PKCE binds code redemption to the client instance that initiated the flow.

steps.title: Do not confuse OAuth with sign-in identity
steps.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework. OpenID Connect adds an authentication/identity layer. An ID token describes authentication to the client; an access token is presented to a resource server according to that API's token contract.

blocks.text: SPA token handling versus a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)

A pure SPA can use an authorization-code flow with PKCE, following the identity provider's current guidance and carefully handling token lifetime, storage and refresh. A BFF keeps OAuth tokens on the server and exposes a browser session to the SPA, reducing direct token exposure to JavaScript but adding server/session and CSRF responsibilities. This is an architecture choice, not a universal winner; choose it based on sensitivity, deployment constraints, identity-provider support and team operations.

blocks.prompt: A React route hides an admin page from non-admin users. What still must happen before an admin API returns protected data?

options.text: Nothing: a hidden route makes the endpoint private
options.feedback: Users can call an API directly, regardless of the rendered route.

options.text: The trusted API/data layer validates the credential and authorizes the requested operation
options.feedback: Authorization is enforced at the resource boundary; the UI guard only improves the navigation experience.

options.text: The frontend decodes a JWT and trusts its payload
options.feedback: Decoding alone does not verify token authenticity, expiry, audience or the API's authorization rules.

options.text: The page must use a longer random URL
options.feedback: An obscure URL is not access control.

blocks.explanation: Keep client navigation checks and server authorization distinct.

blocks.title: Threat-model a protected frontend feature
blocks.context: Review a hypothetical dashboard using sign-in, browser credentials and protected API operations.
instructions: List which component authenticates identity and which layer authorizes access to data.
Compare an SPA code-flow-with-PKCE design and a BFF session design for the feature.
Identify XSS and CSRF risks for the selected credential transport/storage model.
Specify session/token expiry and logout behavior and what the API does after access is revoked.
Write tests for unauthenticated, authenticated-but-forbidden and authorized requests, including direct API calls.
requirements: Authentication and authorization are explicitly distinguished.
No privileged secret is sent to browser JavaScript.
The selected storage/transport model has a threat-model rationale.
Server/data-layer authorization is required regardless of UI guards.
Tests include direct unauthorized requests and session/credential lifecycle cases.

hints: A route guard is UX, not access control.
PKCE protects authorization-code redemption; it does not remove the need to protect tokens and API resources.
HttpOnly cookies reduce JavaScript access but do not automatically prevent CSRF.
successCriteria: Defines the roles of identity provider, client and API.
Explains chosen token/session architecture and threats.
Includes trusted authorization at the data boundary.

items: Authentication proves identity; authorization evaluates a specific operation against policy.
Frontend guards are not security boundaries—validate credentials and permissions at the API/data layer.
Cookie and token designs each have trade-offs; plan for XSS, CSRF, expiry, logout and revocation.
OAuth 2.0 authorization and OpenID Connect identity are related but distinct.
